_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Mathematics unit lecture film, Big Numbers and Below Zero. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow the lesson page's own steps in the lesson's own numbers: 3,406 in its place-value columns (step 4-5), 4,208 regrouped as 3 thousands and 12 hundreds (step 6), 34 x 10 and 34 x 100 (step 7), the thermometer falling from 3 degrees to minus 2 (step 9), minus 2 and minus 9 on the number line (steps 10-11), and 4,630 rounded to the nearest hundred (step 12). Revised 2026-09-24 against a lead review note: five of the longest beats were split (worth, ten-times, and below-zero-in-order each gained a beat) and several others tightened, to bring the average beat sentence from 12.45 to 10.9 words without cutting any teaching. The order chapter's dead 'below' cue (declared, never read by any picture) was given one: the negative half of the number line now glows while 'below zero' is said.
title: Big Numbers and Below Zero
subtitle: Grade 4 Mathematics
objectives: Read and write number names and whole numbers greater than 1000 and less than 0.
Count on and count back in steps of constant size: 1-digit numbers, tens, hundreds or thousands, starting from any number, and extending beyond zero to include negative numbers.
Understand and explain that the value of each digit in numbers is determined by its position in that number.
Use knowledge of place value to multiply and divide whole numbers by 10 and 100.
Compose, decompose and regroup whole numbers.
Understand the relative size of quantities to compare and order positive and negative numbers, using the symbols =, > and <.
Round numbers to the nearest 10, 100, 1000, 10 000 or 100 000.

beats.say: Some numbers are huge, like 47,318. Some sit below zero, like minus 6.
Where a digit stands decides its worth. Today you will read both kinds.
Read this number: three thousand, four hundred and six.

at.name: three thousand, four hundred and six

beats.say: Three thousands, four hundreds, no tens, and six ones.
The zero is not nothing to skip. It holds the tens column open.
Take the zero away and 3,406 turns into 346, a much smaller number.
The same 8 is worth 8 in 58, but 80 in 85.
And eighty thousand in 80,000.
Here is 4,208: four thousands, two hundreds, no tens and eight ones.
Swap one thousand for ten hundreds. That swap is called regrouping.
Now the same number is three thousands, twelve hundreds and eight ones.
It is still 4,208. Regrouping changes how it is stored, never its worth.
Times 10 does not add a zero. Every digit moves one place left.
Take 34 times 10. The 3 tens become 3 hundreds.
The 4 ones become 4 tens, too.
34 times 10 is 340. The zero only fills the empty ones column.
Times 100 moves every digit two places. 34 times 100 is 3,400.
Numbers keep going below zero. A thermometer is where you meet them.
It is 3 degrees, and then it gets 5 degrees colder.
Count down one step at a time: 2, 1, 0, minus 1, minus 2.
The temperature is now minus 2 degrees, two steps below zero.
Zero is a number you pass through, not where counting stops.
On a number line, further right always means bigger.
That keeps working below zero.
Minus 2 sits to the right of minus 9.
Minus 2 is bigger. Minus 9 is nine below zero; minus 2 is two.
Smallest first, these go minus 8, minus 3, zero, then 5.
Rounding asks one question: which neighbour is this number nearer to?
Round 4,630 to the nearest hundred. Its neighbours are 4,600 and 4,700.
It is 30 past 4,600, but 70 short of 4,700.
So 4,630 rounds down to 4,600, the nearer one.
Exactly halfway needs a rule: 4,650 rounds up, to 4,700.
A digit's column decides its worth. A zero holds a column open.
Regroup a thousand into ten hundreds and the number never changes.
Times 10 moves every digit one place to the left.
Below zero, further right is bigger. Rounding picks the nearer neighbour.
